name: Jawline filler

lead: Jawline filler is a non-surgical treatment in which a clinician places a dermal filler, usually HA or CaHA, along the jaw. People get it to add definition to the jaw angle and chin and to soften the look of jowls, and it is often weighed against jaw implants or surgery.

The gel adds volume under the skin along the mandibular angle and border, changing the contour so the line looks sharper or wider once swelling settles. Registered studies include a 180-participant study of a CaHA product, HA products from several manufacturers, and a study of filler in jowls. Users on looksmax.org share before-and-after impressions and maintenance-cost estimates.

paras: A licensed clinician injects along the jaw in an office visit. The filler is gradually absorbed, so people repeat sessions to maintain the look, and it is seen as a lower-commitment, reversible option compared with implants.

Common effects are swelling, bruising and pain. Reviews describe rarer events including contour irregularities, tissue necrosis, vascular occlusion and, in other facial areas, vision loss, and a 2026 case report described sublingual artery occlusion after jawline filler. Fillers are regulated as medical devices.

chain: HA or CaHA added along mandible
angle.text: Jawline filler adds definition to the jaw angle and chin and softens the look of jowls, with a sharper line visible once swelling settles. Hyaluronic acid or CaHA is placed along the mandible to change the contour. It is a non-surgical route people weigh against jaw surgery, and device studies for jawline contouring are registered.

lead: Jawline filler refers to the injection of a dermal filler, most often a hyaluronic acid (HA) or calcium hydroxylapatite (CaHA) product, along the mandible to add definition or volume to the jaw angle, jawline or chin area. It is a non-surgical option used to accentuate a sharper or wider lower face, to address a jawline contour deficit, and to reduce the look of jowls.[1][2][3]

Registered clinical studies have examined fillers for jawline contouring, including a 180-participant study of a CaHA product, HA products from several manufacturers, and a study of filler in jowls.[2][4][5][6][3][7] A 2026 review in Dermatologic Surgery groups jawline filler with temple, nose and lip treatment as high-impact but higher-risk areas, with possible complications ranging from contour irregularities to tissue necrosis, vision loss and embolic events.[1]

In looksmaxxing communities, jawline filler is discussed as a reversible or lower-commitment alternative to jaw implants, and users on looksmax.org share before-and-after impressions and maintenance-cost estimates.[8][9] Research on aesthetic-surgery interest finds that cosmetic procedure interest among men has changed over recent decades, which authors link to declining stigma.[10]

paras: Filler is injected by a clinician along or near the mandibular border to add projection or straighten a perceived contour deficit. HA fillers are made of cross-linked hyaluronic acid, which the body gradually breaks down, while CaHA products are used for firmer volume.[11] Fillers are regulated as medical devices in the United States and require a CE mark in the UK and EEA.[11]

Published reviews of high-risk facial areas discuss anatomy, product selection, injection technique, clinical benefits and complication-mitigation strategies for the jawline alongside the temple, nose and lip.[1]

Registered interventional studies include a completed 180-participant study of a CaHA product to improve jawline contour by adding volume (NCT03583359), completed studies of HA products for jawline contour deficit or jaw volume deficit including a 40-participant study (NCT06336759), a 114-participant post-market follow-up of Decoria Intense Strong (NCT06562075) and a 72-participant study of YVOIRE Y-Solution 720 (NCT04886544).[2][4][5][6]

A 16-participant study examined filler for jowl improvement (NCT04389866), and a phase 4 study of filler for chin profile enhancement in chin regression, asymmetry and jawline contour deficit is recruiting (NCT07777926).[3][7] The published literature identified consists mostly of device registrations and safety-oriented reviews rather than long-term randomized comparisons against surgery, and no results from the registered studies were identified.
Documented harms specific to the area include a case report of vascular occlusion of the sublingual artery after jawline filler injection.[12]

A 2026 review lists risks for filler in high-impact facial regions ranging from contour irregularities to tissue necrosis, vision loss and embolic events.[1] Wikipedia describes common filler effects as bruising, redness, pain and itching, with infection, allergic reactions and lumps less often, and blindness from retrograde embolization rare but usually permanent.[11]
In the jaw region, a case report described occlusion of the sublingual artery, a vessel in the floor of the mouth, after jawline injection.[12]

On looksmax.org, users post accounts of jawline filler results, including one thread in which the original poster described the effect seen one week after swelling had resolved and invited a poll on the outcome.[8] Another user described a filler programme for the gonial angle and chin as a step toward feeling comfortable with their appearance, estimated an ongoing cost of about 1,000 to 2,000 US dollars per year for maintenance, and named jaw implants as an eventual goal, a choice other users questioned.[9]
Commenters in these threads share advice that filler can be dissolved if unwanted, and one reply attributed a cheekbone look to skin being stretched by filler.[8][9]

lore.intro: Jawline filler is discussed on looksmax.org as a non-surgical way to add jaw definition, often as a stepping stone before or instead of implants.[8][9]

claims.claim: Jawline filler gives a visible sharper jaw once swelling settles
Filler is a worthwhile ongoing investment compared with surgery
Filler can be dissolved if unwanted

timeline.event: Study of a CaHA filler for jawline contour (NCT03583359) registered as started.[2]
Several jawline contouring filler studies begin, including HA product studies in the registry.[4][6]
Analysis of 18 years of male interest in aesthetic procedures published.[10]
Review of temple, nose, lip and jawline filler risks and benefits, and a report of sublingual artery occlusion, published.[1][12]
